---
title: "Composite targets and criterion directions"
subtitle: "4.6 · after the postrank vignette m2 and theory book, ch. 12 and 19"
description: "Comparison of reporting objectives based on composite values and criterion-specific directions."
---

Weighting errors on two criteria and comparing a weighted sum of their values can yield opposite directions
for the same pair.

```{=html}
<div id="app" class="prx-app column-page"></div>
<script src="../../js/vendor/d3.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/vendor/plot.min.js"></script>
<script src="../../js/bundles/composite-or-criterion.js"></script>
<script>window.__prxApp = PRX["composite-or-criterion"].mountWidget(document.getElementById("app"));</script>
```

Error weights determine how much a wrong direction on each criterion costs. Composite coefficients determine
how much each target contributes to the combined value. At A = (1, −2) and B = (0, 0), a direction with
less weighted error can therefore run against the order of the equally weighted composite. We compare the
reports under both objectives, holding the withholding cost and available reports fixed.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Different targets.** The criterion-direction costs are .2500, .7500 and .3000 for forward, reverse and
  withholding. The composite costs are 1.0000, 0 and .3000. One objective picks 1/2; the other picks 2/1.
- **Rescale the second criterion.** In **Data and exact values**, A’s composite value becomes .250. Its preferred direction flips.
  The criterion-direction cost .2500 stays the same. The positive multiplier applies to every unit, while error
  weights and composite coefficients keep their separate roles.
- **Composite equality.** Both strict composite directions cost 1.0000. Withholding costs .3000. Each criterion
  still distinguishes the units, but their composite is equal; a shared grade withholds rather than asserting that equality.
- **Two reports, same disclosure.** **Data and exact values** shows the evaluations of all 75 reports. Criterion directions choose
  1/2/2/3 with risk .1417; the composite chooses 1/1/2/3 with risk .0333. Both disclose 5 pairs. Both columns evaluate each selected report under the two objectives.
- **Transform the whole law.** Exponentiating every finite input preserves the criterion best report and its
  risk .1417. The composite now selects 1/1/2/2 with risk .0667. The complete criterion best-report sets before
  and after remain visible under the same settings.
- **Rescale the Normal composite.** The first composite mean is .635. We compute it assuming independence across the six sites and their criteria. Computing the composite uncertainty
  requires the same assumptions about dependence.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
All examples are synthetic supplied laws. Composite coefficients stay nonnegative and sum to one, matching the
package interface. A positive multiplier changes the contribution of a criterion to the composite. A strictly increasing
transformation leaves the ordering within that criterion intact. Choosing which risk to minimize depends on
whether the report concerns individual criterion directions or the composite. The thirty-site marginal releases
leave the joint law undetermined.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
The code computes composite scores from the posterior means, with `weights` as the composite coefficients.
The package divides by the supplied scale, so a second-criterion scale of ten corresponds to a multiplier of .1.

```r
library(postrank)
postrank_composite(pr_tutorial$law$means, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), scales=c(score_A=1,score_B=10))
```
:::
